chapters.title: 6.1 cy.request() Deep Dive
chapters.overviewText: cy.request() fires a real HTTP call from outside the page — Cypress itself talking to the backend, not watching the app's fetch. That is a different mechanism from cy.intercept(). It auto-fails on non-2xx/3xx unless failOnStatusCode is false. Seed via API, verify via UI. Token auth must go through onBeforeLoad (or cy.session()); cookie auth applies Set-Cookie automatically. Playwright's APIRequestContext can hold several isolated identities at once; cy.request() shares one session.
chapters.why: Not testing through the UI what doesn't need the UI is the highest-leverage habit in the manual. Login-bypass mechanics (onBeforeLoad vs cookies) and the Playwright multi-identity gap are interview-grade distinctions.
chapters.when: Before writing any authenticated flow, seeding leave requests, or polling a payroll job. Revisit when localStorage set before visit mysteriously disappears under testIsolation.

practical.scenario: 150 tests need a logged-in manager; one test must POST invalid leave and assert 400; another seeds a leave then spies on the UI GET.
practical.pass: You login with cy.request, thread JWT via onBeforeLoad (or rely on cookies), use failOnStatusCode: false for the 400, and intercept-as-spy after seeding.
practical.fail: You UI-login every test, set localStorage then visit (wiped), or expect cy.request to retry like cy.get without wrapping .should().

chapters.customSummary:
- Runs a real HTTP request outside the app's page context (unlike cy.intercept(), which watches requests the app itself makes) — a genuinely different mechanism, resolves against baseUrl exactly like cy.visit()
- Auto-fails on non-2xx/3xx by default, same philosophy as cy.visit() — catches setup failures immediately instead of producing a confusing UI cascade later. Opt out with failOnStatusCode: false to deliberately test error responses
- Response object auto-parses JSON into .body; also exposes .status, .statusText, .headers, .duration, .isOkStatusCode
- The core pattern: seed via cy.request(), verify via the UI. Skips every UI interaction that isn't the actual thing under test — faster and removes irrelevant flake sources
- Teardown caveat: afterEach cleanup isn't guaranteed to run on a catastrophic stop — prefer "clean before, not clean after" via cy.task() full-reset in before/beforeEach over per-test API-level deletion for anything beyond a single record
- The single highest-leverage use: bypass the login UI. For token auth, must thread the token through onBeforeLoad (setting localStorage before cy.visit() doesn't persist under testIsolation); for cookie auth, cy.request() running in the same browser context applies Set-Cookie automatically — no extra step needed
- Concrete cost: UI login ≈ 3–5s vs API login ≈ 100–300ms; across 150 tests, roughly 10 minutes vs 30 seconds of pure overhead. Full caching layer on top = cy.session() (Part 7.2); full auth patterns = Part 7.4
- Combine with cy.intercept(): seed real data via cy.request(), then spy (not stub) on the UI's own subsequent fetch to assert request shape
- Bulk seeding via a forEach of cy.request() calls works correctly serially, with no Promise.all(), because commands are strictly queued (Part 2.3)
- Polling a backend job: cy.request(url).its('body.status').should('eq', 'completed') — .should() retries the entire preceding chain including the request itself
- vs Playwright: APIRequestContext is a separate, first-class object — you can hold multiple simultaneously (e.g., admin + manager contexts with independent cookies), a genuine structural edge for scenarios needing several concurrent authenticated identities, which cy.request()'s single shared session context can't cleanly match. vs Selenium: zero built-in HTTP capability — requires a fully separate library (requests, RestAssured) bolted on; Cypress/Playwright's same-file, same-language API+UI blend is a real, practical advantage over that split

chapters.title: 6.2 Schema Validation
chapters.overviewText: Value assertions miss contract drift: extra fields, number-to-string changes, missing required keys. For flat objects, Chai's have.all.keys plus type checks suffice. For nested shapes, wrap ajv in a custom command (cy.validateSchema, prevSubject: true, return subject) so it chains. Highest ceiling: pull schemas from a live OpenAPI spec via cy.task() rather than a hand-copied duplicate.
chapters.why: Backend shape changes break frontends with zero frontend commits. Interviewers distinguish live response-schema checks from Pact-style consumer-driven contract tests running in the backend pipeline.
chapters.when: When asserting employee/leave API contracts, wrapping ajv as a command, or deciding whether to duplicate a schema vs reading openapi.yaml.

practical.scenario: GET /api/employees/123 must match the published employee contract, including nested manager.
practical.pass: You compile an ajv schema with additionalProperties: false, chain .its('body').validateSchema(employeeSchema), and fail with the ajv path.
practical.fail: You only expect(body.id).to.eq(123), or throw from a command without returning the subject so the chain dies.

chapters.customSummary:
- Goes beyond checking specific field values — verifies the entire shape of a response, catching drift (extra fields, type changes, missing required fields) that silently breaks a frontend with zero frontend code changes
- Manual/Chai approach for simple flat shapes: expect(body).to.have.all.keys(...) (fails on any extra/missing key), plus .to.be.a(), .to.match(), .to.be.oneOf() — no dependency needed, but unwieldy for nested/variable shapes
- ajv-based validation is the standard heavier-duty approach: define a JSON Schema per endpoint, wrap it in a custom command (cy.validateSchema(schema), registered with { prevSubject: true } — mechanics in Part 8.1) so it chains naturally and reports ajv's precise error path on failure
- Works identically for array/list responses ({ type: 'array', items: itemSchema }) and can validate both request and response shapes for one endpoint
- Highest-ceiling approach: derive the schema from a live OpenAPI/Swagger spec rather than a hand-maintained duplicate — this catches the backend's actual drift from its own published contract, not just drift from a test-author's frozen assumption. Implemented via a cy.task() that extracts the relevant schema from the spec file at Node level
- Scoping note: this is response-shape validation at test-run time against a live API — genuinely different from (and lighter-weight than) formal consumer-driven contract testing (Pact-style), which runs in the backend's own CI pipeline. Worth knowing the distinction exists; building a full Pact setup is out of this manual's scope (Part 0.8)
- vs Playwright: functionally a wash — neither has schema validation built in; both reach for the same ajv library. Cypress needs a small custom-command wrapper for chaining; Playwright's Node-native test code calls ajv directly with none needed
- vs Selenium (paired with Python/Java): jsonschema (Python) is equivalent; RestAssured (Java) has schema validation as a genuinely first-class, built-in feature (matchesJsonSchema()), arguably more polished out of the box than either JS tool's DIY-via-ajv approach — unsurprising, since RestAssured was purpose-built for API testing from day one

chapters.title: 6.3 Combining UI + API Tests
chapters.overviewText: Every UI step that isn't the thing under test is cost without benefit. Five patterns: (1) API seed, UI verify; (2) API before and after, UI only for the click; (3) deliberate full-UI smoke; (4) spy (not stub) on the real payload the UI sends; (5) simulate another actor with a mid-test cy.request() for races Cypress can't do with two tabs. Over-stubbing verifies only that a component renders given props.
chapters.why: The mix — mostly Pattern 1, a layer of pure API contracts, a small tagged smoke set — is what a healthy suite looks like. Pattern 5 is the honest answer to 'how do you test two managers racing?' given Cypress's single-tab model.
chapters.when: When designing leave-approval, onboarding, or payroll coverage, and whenever a spec is slow because it fills the same form three times as setup.

practical.scenario: Prove a manager sees only their team's pending leave, that approval decrements balance, and that a conflict banner appears if another manager already approved.
practical.pass: You seed three requests via API (Pattern 1), assert balance via API after the UI click (Pattern 2), and mid-test PUT-approve as the other manager (Pattern 5).
practical.fail: You submit three leaves through the UI as setup, or stub GET leave-balance with { annual: 15 } and call that an E2E test.

chapters.customSummary:
- Core principle: every UI step that isn't the thing under test is cost without benefit — slower, an extra flake surface, and it obscures what's actually being verified
- Decision framework: form/component itself → UI · data-display correctness → API seed + UI verify · multi-step flow where only one step matters → API for the rest, UI for that step · pure API contract → no UI at all · true end-to-end proof → full UI, deliberately, as a small minority
- Pattern 1 (the workhorse): seed via cy.request(), assert via the rendered UI — e.g., verifying a manager sees only their team's requests by seeding three requests across two managers via API and checking the rendered count
- Pattern 2: API before AND after the step under test, UI only for the exact interaction being verified — and the final assertion often goes back through the API (e.g., checking a recalculated balance) rather than parsing it out of the DOM, since that's more precise and faster for a backend concern
- Pattern 3 — deliberate full-UI smoke tests: a small, tagged (@smoke, Part 10.1) set per feature that exercises the real path end to end, because these are the only tests that catch a broken form field or misrouted submit handler that shortcut patterns structurally cannot. Even here, non-central steps (like login) still get shortcut via API — the discipline is "shortcut everything except the thing under test," not "never shortcut"
- Pattern 4: spy (not stub) on the real network call the UI makes, letting a real backend respond, specifically to assert the request payload is constructed correctly — a distinct concern from response-shape validation (6.2) or display-correctness (Pattern 1)
- Pattern 5: race-condition / cross-actor scenarios — simulate "another manager" as a plain mid-test cy.request() call rather than trying to coordinate two real browser sessions, which Cypress's single-tab-per-test model (Part 0.6) can't do reliably anyway
- The opposite anti-pattern: over-stubbing everything verifies only "does my component render given props," not whether the real backend's response shape matches frontend expectations — exactly what 6.2's schema validation and Pattern 3's smoke tests exist to catch. A healthy suite mixes all three registers: mostly Pattern-1-style API-seeded/UI-verified tests, a meaningful layer of pure API contract tests, and a small deliberate set of full-stack smoke tests
- vs Playwright: same strategic principle applies identically; the capability gap from 6.1 (independent simultaneous APIRequestContexts) becomes concretely relevant specifically for Pattern-5-style multi-actor scenarios — achievable in Cypress via a plain extra cy.request() call, but doesn't scale as cleanly to many simultaneous distinct identities as Playwright's model does. vs Selenium: the seed-via-API/verify-via-UI discipline is tool-agnostic and predates all three frameworks — what differs is purely ergonomics: Cypress and Playwright blend both concerns in one file/language/assertion-library natively, while Selenium achieves the same discipline only by importing a second, separate tool into the same test
